claims.text: Engineered coherent nanoprecipitates at grain boundaries enhance dislocation climb in tungsten-based refractory alloys at approximately 800 °C.
Enhanced dislocation climb produces greater high-temperature plastic strain.
Enhanced dislocation climb improves the toughness of tungsten-based refractory alloys.
The proposed nanoprecipitates lower local energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Nanoprecipitate-facilitated dislocation climb relieves stress concentrations.
Nanoprecipitate-facilitated dislocation climb delays strain localization.
Delayed strain localization enables sustained plastic deformation at high temperature.
High-temperature plastic deformation can be controlled by dislocation activity.
Initial microstructure and applied temperature, strain, and strain rate influence high-temperature plastic response.
The controlled comparison should vary the presence of engineered grain-boundary nanoprecipitates while holding grain size, defect density, and other microstructural parameters constant.
Approximately 800 °C is representative of high-temperature fusion plasma-facing operation.
Testing with thermal gradients and irradiation can simulate fusion plasma-facing operational conditions.
Specimens containing the engineered nanoprecipitates will exhibit higher dislocation climb rates than the unperturbed baseline.
Specimens containing the engineered nanoprecipitates will exhibit greater plastic strain capacity than the unperturbed baseline.
Specimens containing the engineered nanoprecipitates will exhibit greater toughness than the unperturbed baseline.
Prior evidence suggests that nanoprecipitates can influence dislocation behavior.
The hypothesis may not apply outside the vicinity of 800 °C or under substantially different irradiation conditions.
Failure to obtain statistically significant increases in climb rate, plastic strain capacity, and toughness relative to the controlled baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
